note: b has no puff of air. To English ears it can sound halfway between b and p.
p has a strong puff of air, as in English "pie".
d has no puff of air. The final ui sounds like "way".
t has a strong puff of air. The final ian sounds like "yen", not "ee-ahn".
g has no puff of air, like the k in "skip". ou sounds like "oh".
k has a strong puff of air, as in "kite".
j is like the j in "jeep", with the tip of the tongue down behind the lower teeth.
q sounds like the ch in "cheese". After q, u is really ü.
x is like "sh" said with a smile, never "ks". Doubled, 谢谢 is "thank you".
zh is like the j in "judge" with the tongue curled back. As in 中国 (China).
ch is like the ch in "church" with the tongue curled back. The i just buzzes: not "chee".
sh with the tongue curled back, and the i is a buzz. Not "shee".
r here is like the s in "measure"; the vowel just buzzes. Not "ree".
z sounds like the ds in "kids", and the i buzzes.
c sounds like the ts in "cats", never like k.
s is a plain s, and ui sounds like "way": close to English "sway".
e sounds like the "uh" in "duh", not "eh". h is rougher than English h.
ü: say "ee" and round your lips. Written with the dots after l and n.
First tone: high and level, as if singing one note.
Second tone: it rises, like a surprised "Huh?" Set: 妈 麻 马 骂.
Third tone: low. Said alone it dips and rises; before another tone it stays low.
Fourth tone: falls sharply, like a firm "No!"
Third tone. Same letters as 卖 (mài, to sell): the tone changes the deal.
Fourth tone: it falls. Mix up 买 and 卖 and you swap buyer and seller.
First tone, high and level. With a rising tone it becomes 糖, sugar.
Second tone: it rises. Said flat and high it is 汤, soup.
Fourth tone: it falls. Said low, it becomes 吻 (to kiss).
Third tone: low. 我可以问你吗？ (May I ask you?) said with a low 问 asks for a kiss.
First tone. The same letters with other tones: 盐 (salt) rises, 眼 (eye) dips.
Second tone: it rises. Said flat and high it is 烟, smoke.
Third tone: low. In speech usually 眼睛 (yǎnjing).
First tone. With a low third tone it is 起 (to get up); with a falling fourth tone, 气 (air).

meaning: to get up (as in 起床)
note: Third tone: low. 起床 is to get out of bed.
Fourth tone: it falls. 生气 is to get angry.
Third tone: low. 又 (again) has the falling fourth tone.
Fourth tone: it falls. 有 (to have) is the low third tone.
Looks like a person walking: two legs.
Also the measure word for family members: 四口人.
Two trees make 林 (woods), three make 森 (forest).
Two trees side by side. Also a common family name.
Three trees: more than a wood. Usually said 森林.
Three peaks on a line.
Drawn from a crescent moon. 一月 is January.
日 (sun) + 月 (moon). In 明天 it means "next" (tomorrow).
On the left of a character it hints at women: 妈, 姐, 妹.
A baby with its arms out. Also a common noun ending: 饺子, 桌子.
女 (woman) + 子 (child).
亻 (person) + 木 (tree): a person resting against a tree. As in 休息.
A mark above a line. 桌子上 is "on the table".
A mark below a line. 下雨 is "it's raining": rain comes down.
A two-panel door, simplified. In traditional characters: 門.
Drops of rain falling under the sky.
A flame with two sparks. 火车 (fire + vehicle) is a train.
A stream with splashes. On the left of a character it becomes 氵: 汤, 酒.
Safe with anyone. To an older person or a customer: 您好！
您 is the polite "you": for older people, teachers and customers.
To a group or a class. 大家 means everybody.
Students greet the teacher by title, not by name.
For the morning. Friends often just say 早！
Only when someone is going to bed, not as an evening hello.
A friendly catch-up. 你好吗？ is a real question about how someone is.
Literally "knowing you, I'm very happy". 很高兴认识你 is just as common. To someone older: 认识您很高兴。
Among family and close friends Chinese says thank you less than English does.
To an older person, a teacher or a customer.
Literally "don't be polite". bú, because 客 has the fourth tone.
A real apology: you bumped into someone, broke something, came late.
The answer to 对不起 (sorry).
For small things: getting attention, squeezing past, a short wait. Lighter than 对不起.

meaning: It's nothing. / Don't worry about it.
note: A casual answer to thanks or to a small apology.
Opens a question to a stranger: 请问，地铁站在哪儿？
Literally "again see".
A day + 见: 星期一见 is "see you Monday".
Like 妈妈, the second syllable has the neutral tone.
The second 妈 has the neutral tone: māma.
There is no word for just "brother": older is 哥哥, younger is 弟弟.
Younger sister: 妹妹.
Older brother: 哥哥.
Older sister: 姐姐.
Mom's father has his own word: 姥爷 or 外公.
Mom's mother has her own word: 姥姥 or 外婆.
子 here has the neutral tone.
女 (woman) + 儿 (child).
我朋友 and 我的朋友 both mean "my friend".
们 makes a plural for people: 我们, 你们, 他们.
For men or mixed groups. Women only: 她们. Both are said tāmen.

meaning: How many people are in your family?
note: 几 asks for a small number; 口 counts family members.

meaning: There are four people in my family.
note: 口 is the measure word for family members.
Number + measure word + noun. Two older brothers: 两个哥哥.

meaning: I don't have any brothers or sisters.
note: 没有, never 不有.
Also for a family friend, a neighbor or a cleaner. For a man: 叔叔.
叫 = to be called. Chinese names put the family name first.
To a peer or a child. 什么 (what) sits where the answer goes.
Answer 我姓王 (my surname is Wang), not 我贵姓.
姓 = to have the surname. The usual answer to 您贵姓？
Country + 人 (person): 美国人, 中国人.
Literally "you are which-country person?"
不 before 是 is said bú, because 是 has the fourth tone.
也 (also) goes before the verb, never at the end like "too".
都 (all) goes after the subject and before the verb.
With 住 (live), 在 + place comes after the verb; with most verbs it goes before.
哪儿 (where) takes the place of the answer. Also: 你住哪儿？
No 是 and no "years old" verb: just the number + 岁.

meaning: How old are you? (to an adult)
note: To a child: 你几岁？
中文 is the Chinese language; 汉语 means the same. 学习 (study) also works: 我学习中文.
喜欢 + verb, with no word for "to" in between.
爱好 = hobby. 看书, "look at books", is to read.
Close family usually takes no 的: 我爸爸.
It also fills a gap inside a number: 一百零五 (105).
Said this way when counting. Before other words its tone changes: 一个, 一杯.
For counting, phone numbers and inside bigger numbers: 十二, 二十.
两个人, 两杯茶. Counting and in bigger numbers: 二 (十二, 二十).
Second tone. Easy to mix up with 四 (sì, four): listen for the sh.
Ten + five. Fifty is 五十: five tens.
Two tens. Twenty-one: 二十一.
Nine tens and nine: the top of the two-digit pattern.
一百五 is 150, short for 一百五十. 105 is 一百零五.
零 marks the empty tens place.
Chinese groups big numbers by four zeros: 100,000 is 十万, ten ten-thousands.
多少 asks for any amount; 几 is only for small numbers you expect to be under ten.
钱 (money) often follows the amount in speech: 十块钱.
块 in speech, 元 on price tags.
毛 is a tenth of a yuan, in speech; on price tags it is 角.
Short for 三块五毛: the last unit is often dropped.
个 is the all-purpose measure word, but many nouns have their own.
本 for books and notebooks. Not 三书.
杯 for cups and glasses: 一杯水, 两杯茶.
张 for flat things: tickets, tables, photos, paper.
只 (zhī) for most animals. The same character read zhǐ means "only".
只 again, for animals. 两, not 二, before a measure word.
条 for long, thin things: fish, roads, pants.
件 for clothes, especially tops and jackets.
双 = a pair: shoes, socks, chopsticks.
瓶 = bottle.
辆 for cars, bikes and buses.
位 is the polite measure word for people.
家 for shops, restaurants and companies.
这 + measure word: 这个, 这本书.
那 + measure word + noun. 张 for tables, because the top is flat.
No number needed: 这 + measure word + noun. Not 这书.
几 + measure word asks for a small number. Restaurant staff ask politely: 几位？
Northern family food, eaten at Chinese New Year.
Filled with meat or vegetables; a classic breakfast.
饭 alone also means a meal: 吃饭 is to eat.
A pot of broth on the table where everyone cooks their own meat and vegetables.
Wrapped in thin pancakes with sauce and scallions.
碗 (bowl) is the measure word.
红茶, literally "red tea", is black tea.

meaning: What do you want to eat?
note: 想 = would like. 什么 goes where the answer goes, after the verb.
我要 is normal when ordering; 请给我 is softer.

meaning: We'll have a Kung Pao chicken.
note: 来 + amount + dish is a very common way to order.
点菜 = to order dishes.
Literally "don't want the spicy kind". A little spicy: 微辣.
Say it when the server asks how spicy you want a dish.
不 for habits and choices.
Beer often comes in big bottles to share.
了 shows a change: you weren't full before, now you are.

meaning: Can I get this to go?
note: 打包 = to pack up leftovers or takeout.
Call the server 服务员, never 小姐.
太 + adjective + 了: too.

meaning: Could you make it a bit cheaper?
note: Fine in markets, not in malls or supermarkets.

meaning: Can I pay by scanning a code?
note: Most shops in China are paid by phone: you scan the shop's code.

meaning: Do you have it in a large?
note: Sizes: 大号, 中号, 小号.
Literally "I'll look a little": a doubled verb softens it.

meaning: How much is this (piece of clothing)?
note: 件 is the measure word for tops and jackets: 这件衣服.
一共 = in total. Ask this at the checkout.
Point and say it: you don't need to know the name of the thing.
试试 is a doubled verb: "give it a try".
别的 = other, different.

meaning: Do you have a smaller one?
note: Adjective + 一点儿 = a little more so: 大一点儿, 便宜一点儿.
Once you both know it's clothing, 这件 is enough: no need to repeat 衣服.
打折 = give a discount. On signs, 八折 means you pay 80%, i.e. 20% off.

meaning: Can I pay by credit card?
note: Big stores and hotels take cards; small shops often take only phone payments.
现金 = cash. Small shops may not have much change.

meaning: I'd like to buy a pair of shoes.
note: 双 is the measure word for pairs: 一双鞋, 一双筷子.
A polite way to leave without buying anything.

meaning: I don't want it after all.
note: 了 here shows a change of mind.
Time words go before the verb: 我明天去.
Weekday = 星期 + number; Sunday is 星期天 or 星期日.
点 = o'clock. Two o'clock is 两点, not 二点.
半 = half.
Month first, then day: big to small. In writing 日 often replaces 号.
几 asks for the number: literally "today is week-which-number?"
号 is the day of the month in speech.
With days and dates you can leave out 是.
The day before yesterday is 前天; the day after tomorrow, 后天.
星期六 and 星期天 together.
分 = minutes. Two o'clock is always 两点, never 二点.
一刻 = a quarter of an hour. You can also say 八点十五.
Part of the day first, then the hour: big to small.
小时 is usually said with the measure word 个: 一个小时, 两个小时.
分钟 counts minutes directly, with no 个.

meaning: I get up at seven every day.
note: When it happens goes before the verb: 每天七点起床.
Literally "we Saturday meet": the day goes before 见.

meaning: What time do you get off work?
note: 几点 sits where the answer will go, before the verb.
Thing + 在 + 哪儿. Also 厕所 (more direct).
Also 一直走.
Right: 右拐.

meaning: The bank is next to the supermarket.
note: The place word comes after its noun: 超市旁边.

meaning: Is there a subway station nearby?
note: Place first, then 有: "nearby has…".

meaning: on the right; the right side
note: Left: 左边. 在右边 = it's on the right.

meaning: The hospital is across from the bank.
note: 对面 (opposite) goes after the place it is opposite: 银行对面.
Where (在路口) comes before the action (右拐).
离 = away from. Answers: 不远 (not far), 很近 (close).
Literally "walk five minutes".

meaning: Excuse me, how do I get to Tiananmen?
note: 去 + place + 怎么走: the standard way to ask the way.
就 adds "right, exactly".
前边 = in front, ahead; 后边 = behind.
Literally "red-green light".
马路 = road; literally "horse road".

meaning: I'm going to the supermarket to buy some things.
note: Two verbs in a row: 去 + place + what you do there. No word for "to".

meaning: I'll wait for you at the park.
note: The place with 在 goes before the verb 等 (wait).
In Taiwan: 計程車. Most people now book rides on an app.
Pay with your phone or a transit card.

meaning: To the airport, please. (to a driver)
note: 师傅 is the polite way to address a driver.

meaning: I'm taking the high-speed train to Shanghai.
note: How you travel goes before 去: 坐高铁去.
The destination describes the ticket, so it comes before 票 with 的.
In Taiwan: 公車.
In Taiwan: 腳踏車. Shared bikes are unlocked by scanning a code.
Big cities have several: check which one your train leaves from.

meaning: to fly; to take a plane
note: 坐 (sit) is the verb for vehicles you ride in: 坐车, 坐地铁. Bikes take 骑 (ride).
Hotels ask for it at check-in.
Noun + 呢: "where's…?" when you can't find something.
One piece of luggage: 一件行李.
At a hotel front desk.
一下 softens a request: "just for a moment".
打车 = get a taxi, or book a ride on an app.

meaning: What time does the train arrive?
note: 几点 goes before the verb 到 (arrive).
了 at the end shows a change: now we're here.

meaning: I'm going to Xi'an for a trip.
note: 旅游 = travel for fun. A business trip is 出差.
Also how you address your teacher: 王老师, or just 老师.
College student: 大学生.
Where you work goes before 工作.
Literally "you do what work?"

meaning: I can speak a little Chinese.
note: 会 for a skill you learned.
No word for "a": just 是 + the job.
同 = same: 同事 (same work), 同学 (classmate).
Counted with 家: 一家公司.
The owner of a small shop is 老板.
在 before a verb: in the middle of doing it, now or these days.
在 + verb for right now. Not 你是做什么.

meaning: I'm in a meeting right now.
note: 正在 stresses "right at this moment".
会 for a learned skill: driving, swimming, a language.
能 = able to (time, health, permission); 会 is for skills you learned.
可以 = may, it's allowed.
No word for "there": time + 有 + thing.
上课 = have class; class ends: 下课.
馆 = a building for something, as in 饭馆 and 咖啡馆.
Where does it hurt? 你哪儿不舒服？
Body part + 疼: 肚子疼 (stomachache).
了 here shows a change: I've caught a cold.
药 = medicine.
For emergencies only. For everyday help: 请帮我一下.
了 shows the change: I've come down with a fever.
肚子 = belly. No "my" needed: 我肚子疼.

meaning: What's wrong? / Where does it hurt?
note: What a doctor asks. Literally "where are you not comfortable?"

meaning: I'd like to see a doctor.
note: 看医生 = see a doctor; 看病 also works.

meaning: I have a bit of a cough.
note: 有点儿 = a bit, usually about something unwelcome.
一下 makes the request lighter: "for a moment".
别 + verb = don't.
Shouted as a warning, or said kindly: 路上小心 (take care on the way).
The standard advice for any illness, together with 多休息 (rest a lot).
吧 makes it friendly advice, not an order.

meaning: Are you feeling a bit better?
note: Adjective + 一点儿 + 了: a bit more so now.

Emergency numbers: 110 for the police, 120 for an ambulance.
Also "old" for age: 你多大？ (how old are you?)
小王: a friendly way to call a younger person named Wang.
好吃 = good to eat; 好喝 = good to drink.
No 是 before an adjective; 很 is often just glue, not "very".
Not 她是高.
帅 is the everyday word for a good-looking man.

真 + adjective = really, so: an exclamation.
Weather words work like other adjectives: 很热, no 是.
很 is light here. For "very busy", say 非常忙.
不 + adjective, with no 是: not 中文不是难.
不 + adjective, no 是. 不 before a fourth tone is bú: bú dà.
热闹 = busy, noisy and fun. Quiet: 安静.
菜 = a dish, or vegetables.
有点儿 + adjective: a bit, and you don't like it.
A longer describer goes before the noun, linked by 的: 很好的人.
The color goes before the noun, linked by 的; 辆 is the measure word for cars.

Asks the same question back.

Often paired with 虽然 (although) later on; at A1 it stands alone.

meaning: How is it? / How about it?
note: 你最近怎么样？ = How have you been lately?

哪 (third tone) = which; 那 (fourth tone) = that.
吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question. Answer 忙 or 不忙, not 是.
Verb + 不 + verb asks yes or no. Never add 吗 to it.
有没有 is the verb-not-verb form of 有.
With a two-character verb: 喜不喜欢 or 喜欢不喜欢.

meaning: How do you say this in Chinese?
note: 怎么 + verb = how to do it.
Often paired: 因为…所以… (because … so …).
Chinese can use "because" and "so" in one sentence; English picks one.
或者 for "or" in a statement; in a question, use 还是.

meaning: He and I are going together.
note: 和 joins nouns (我和他); 一起 goes before the verb.
Not 我是高兴: adjectives take 很, not 是.
没 for what did not happen, with no 了: not 我没去了. (我不去了 means "I'm not going any more".)
两 before a measure word, never 二个人.
Not 小姐, which now suggests a sex worker in the mainland.
A friendly hello among people who know each other, not an invitation.
Not 我是累: no 是 before an adjective.
No 是 and no "years old" verb: number + 岁.
了 shows the change: I've gotten hungry. Not 我是饿.
不 for habits and choices; 没 for what didn't happen.
有 always takes 没, never 不: not 我不有钱.

It asks how you really are. For a casual hi, just say 你好.

不…了 = a change of plan. Not the same as 我没去 (I didn't go).
Don't use it to call anyone in the mainland: it can suggest a sex worker. Fine in Taiwan.
With 西 in the neutral tone it means "thing"; said with two full tones it means "east and west".
Everyday slang, usually friendly, but not for formal use. Literally "old outsider".

中国人 = a Chinese person; 中国菜 = Chinese food.
After the surname: 王先生. Can also mean "husband".

什么时候 = when; 小的时候 = as a child.

Fuller form of 事: 这件事情.

有钱 = rich; 多少钱？ = how much?
回家 = go home. Also a measure word for shops.
Surname first: 王明 is Mr. Wang.
什么意思？ = what does it mean?
这个地方 = this place.
The everyday word; 电话 is a call or a landline.

Lit. "electric brain".
看电视 = watch TV.
看电影 = see a movie.
Measure word 件 for a top.
买房子 = buy a home.
我的房间 = my room.
去学校 = go to school.
去医院 = go to the hospital.
看医生 = see a doctor.
Casual: 男的.
Casual: 女的; polite: 女士.
Casual: 老公.
Casual: 老婆.

Affectionate, not rude.
More formal than 爸爸妈妈.
我的家人 = my family.
世界上 = in the world.
哪个国家？ = which country?
大城市 = a big city.
走路 = to walk.
开车 = drive. Measure word 辆.

吃饭 = eat (a meal).
喝茶 = drink tea.
一杯咖啡 = a cup of coffee.
Measure word 本: 三本书.
说话 = talk.
上课 = attend class.
汉语 is the textbook word.

洗手 = wash your hands.

听音乐 = listen to music.
玩游戏 = play games.
送礼物 = give a gift.

Polite; 老外 is casual.
A friendly way to address a stall owner.

Measure word 只.

吃水果 = eat fruit.

Pork, unless named: 牛肉 = beef.

面 = flour or noodles.
一杯牛奶.

桌子上 = on the table.

Blunt; 洗手间 is politer.

The app everyone in China uses to message and pay.
上网 = go online.
电话号码 = phone number.

Erhua, said in the north.

Opposite of 小孩儿.

吃药 = take medicine.

我不知道。 For people, use 认识.

让我看看 = let me see.

meaning: to want to; to think; to miss
note: 我想去 = I want to go. 想你 = miss you.
可以吗？ = is that OK?
做饭 = cook; 做完 = finish doing.
等一下 = wait a moment. After a list: etc.
